slides.title: An address needs a context and a lifetime
keyPoints: The same number can mean different storage
Mappings can change while a process remains alive
A pointer is not a permanent object identity
slides.narration: Think of apartment number twelve without a building name. The number alone does not identify a home. A virtual address similarly needs an address-space context. It also needs a time: a mapping can be removed and a later object can occupy the same range. This is why comparing numeric addresses across processes does not prove sharing, and why keeping a pointer after its object dies is unsafe even if the bytes remain mapped. The compiler checks pointer types, while the operating system checks mappings and permissions. Neither check alone proves the full lifetime contract a C++ program requires.

slides.title: Use an offset when a shared region moves
keyPoints: An offset names a position relative to a region
Each participant adds its own base
Validate the offset before forming an address
slides.narration: This arithmetic model has two views of the same sixteen-byte region, one starting at one thousand and the other at five thousand. Both use offset twelve, so their numeric locations are one thousand twelve and five thousand twelve. The offset remains twelve in each view. Offset sixteen is rejected because it is just past the region, not a byte inside it. These integers are not actual pointers and the program performs no memory mapping. The model isolates the representation choice: sharing an offset can survive different virtual bases, while copying one participant’s raw address cannot. A real implementation must also check object alignment, size, and synchronization.

slides.title: Private and shared describe permitted observations
keyPoints: Private modification must not change another private view
Shared storage deliberately permits communication
Physical duplication is an implementation detail
slides.narration: A private mapping can initially share physical backing through copy-on-write. That does not mean one process is allowed to change another process’s logically private value. The operating system preserves private modification when a writer needs a separate view. A shared mapping has a different contract: changes to common storage may be visible through another mapping under the platform’s synchronization rules. Therefore, count neither physical copies nor pointer values as the definition of privacy. Ask which observations the program is allowed to make after a store. This distinction becomes important when reviewing memory use: shared backing may save storage without changing the private behavior visible to applications.

question.prompt: Can two private mappings temporarily share physical storage?
question.answer: Yes, provided the system preserves logically private modification, for example using copy-on-write.

slides.title: Two real mappings can reach one backing byte
keyPoints: Two mmap calls create separate views in one process
MAP_SHARED connects both to the same file byte
The demonstration prints equality of effects, not addresses
slides.narration: This Linux/POSIX demonstration creates a temporary one-byte file, removes its directory name, and maps it twice with shared access. The two mapping addresses are distinct, but both refer to the same backing byte. Writing Q through the first view lets the second view read Q. The printed true reports distinct views, not two independent files. Both mappings are released and the descriptor is closed on the successful path. This is a real mapping demonstration within one process; it does not claim to create two processes or implement a cross-process synchronization protocol. A production wrapper should also release already acquired resources when an intermediate call fails.

slides.eyebrow: SOURCE CONCEPT · REASON THROUGH THE MECHANISM
keyPoints: A virtual address is interpreted in an address-space context.
The same numeric address in two processes can designate unrelated objects.
The meaning of an address also changes over time when a mapping is removed and another mapping occupies the same range.
Do not infer usable address-space size from pointer size alone.
slides.narration:
A virtual address is interpreted in an address-space context. The same numeric address in two processes can designate unrelated objects. The meaning of an address also changes over time when a mapping is removed and another mapping occupies the same range. Do not infer usable address-space size from pointer size alone. A 64-bit pointer representation does not imply that all 64 bits are available as independent implemented virtual-address bits. x86-64 configurations support particular address widths and canonical-address rules. The examples here use explicitly stated simplified widths rather than treating one hardware configuration as universal.

In plain English: Think of an address written on a note: the note can tell you where to look, but it does not prove the thing is still there or that you are allowed to use it.

slides.title: Physical addresses
slides.eyebrow: SOURCE CONCEPT · REASON THROUGH THE MECHANISM
keyPoints: A physical address identifies a location in the processor’s physical address map.
That map can include ordinary memory and regions associated with devices; physical does not mean that every possible address corresponds to an installed DRAM byte.
The operating system manages physical frames and establishes mappings that connect them to virtual pages.
Applications normally neither choose arbitrary frames nor rely on a mapping remaining attached to one frame forever.
slides.narration:
A physical address identifies a location in the processor’s physical address map. That map can include ordinary memory and regions associated with devices; physical does not mean that every possible address corresponds to an installed DRAM byte. The operating system manages physical frames and establishes mappings that connect them to virtual pages. Applications normally neither choose arbitrary frames nor rely on a mapping remaining attached to one frame forever. Moving or replacing backing storage is possible as long as the required observable behavior is preserved and the translation machinery is updated correctly.

In plain English: Think of an address written on a note: the note can tell you where to look, but it does not prove the thing is still there or that you are allowed to use it.

slides.title: Address translation
slides.eyebrow: SOURCE CONCEPT · REASON THROUGH THE MECHANISM
keyPoints: Translation maps a virtual address to a physical address while checking the requested access.
A useful teaching decomposition is virtual address = virtual page number + page offset .
The page number selects a mapping; the offset identifies the byte within that page.
With equal-sized pages and frames, translation preserves the offset.
slides.narration:
Translation maps a virtual address to a physical address while checking the requested access. A useful teaching decomposition is virtual address = virtual page number + page offset . The page number selects a mapping; the offset identifies the byte within that page. With equal-sized pages and frames, translation preserves the offset. Translation is therefore not an arbitrary byte-by-byte lookup. Contiguous bytes within one mapped page share the same mapping and permissions at the paging granularity. An access that spans a page boundary can involve more than one translation and can encounter different permissions on the two pages.

In plain English: Think of an address written on a note: the note can tell you where to look, but it does not prove the thing is still there or that you are allowed to use it.

slides.title: Shared memory
slides.eyebrow: SOURCE CONCEPT · REASON THROUGH THE MECHANISM
keyPoints: Shared memory deliberately maps common storage into more than one execution environment.
A store through one mapping can become visible through another according to the platform’s memory and synchronization rules.
This avoids copying every message through a separate transfer buffer, but it does not remove the need for a communication protocol.
Shared-memory programs must define ownership, synchronization, initialization, and recovery from participant failure.

slides.eyebrow: SOURCE CONCEPT · REASON THROUGH THE MECHANISM
keyPoints: Assume 4-KiB pages.
Process A maps virtual page 4 to physical frame 12; process B maps virtual page 4 to physical frame 27.
Both load from virtual address 0x4123 .
The virtual page number is 0x4 , and the offset is 0x123 .
slides.narration: Assume 4-KiB pages. Process A maps virtual page 4 to physical frame 12; process B maps virtual page 4 to physical frame 27. Both load from virtual address 0x4123 . The virtual page number is 0x4 , and the offset is 0x123 . A reaches physical address 0xC123 ; B reaches 0x1B123 . The same pointer bits do not imply shared data. Now suppose A maps virtual page 8 and B maps virtual page 9 to physical frame 30. A’s 0x8080 and B’s 0x9080 both identify physical address 0x1E080 . These calculations illustrate two independent properties: equal virtual addresses can refer to different storage, and different virtual addresses can refer to shared storage. They say nothing by themselves about access permission or synchronization. A correct access requires the mapping and the requested operation to be allowed.

slides.title: Translation preserves the position within a page
keyPoints: Split page number from page offset
Map the page; retain the offset
Adjacent virtual pages need not have adjacent frames
slides.narration: With four-thousand-ninety-six-byte pages, address four thousand one hundred is page one with offset four. If page one maps to frame seven, translation selects frame seven’s base and keeps offset four. It does not independently choose a new physical location for every byte. The next byte in that same page keeps the same frame mapping, but crossing the page boundary may select a completely different frame. A contiguous C++ array can therefore span noncontiguous physical frames without changing its indexing behavior. Conversely, remaining inside one mapped page does not make an out-of-bounds array index legal in C++.

question.answer: The offset within the page remains unchanged.

slides.title: A 64-bit pointer does not promise 64 implemented address bits
keyPoints: Representation width differs from implemented virtual width
Canonical rules depend on the platform
Use a stated model for bit calculations
slides.narration: A pointer may occupy eight bytes while the machine implements a smaller virtual-address space with rules for the remaining bits. The chapter discusses particular x86-64 configurations rather than treating one address width as universal. For arithmetic exercises, write the assumed width explicitly: a thirty-two-bit model with four-kibibyte pages has twelve offset bits and twenty page-number bits. slides.title: Physical addresses include more than installed DRAM
keyPoints: The physical map may contain device regions
Not every possible physical address names RAM
Applications normally request mappings rather than frames
slides.narration: Physical means interpreted in the processor’s physical address map. It does not mean every possible numeric address corresponds to an installed DRAM byte. Some ranges refer to devices, and some may not be populated. Ordinary application code usually requests memory through an allocation or mapping interface; the kernel chooses and manages backing frames. That backing can change while the required visible behavior remains stable. A program that treats a virtual pointer as a physical device address has crossed an interface boundary without authorization from the platform. Device I/O needs its own mapping and access rules, including ordering rules that ordinary memory examples do not supply.
actions: Predict the result and name the mapping or invariant that supports it before revealing the answer.

question.prompt: Why is a virtual pointer not a suitable physical address for a device command?
question.answer: Translation and device addressing have distinct contracts; the platform must establish the required physical or device-visible mapping.

slides.title: Shared storage does not provide a message protocol
keyPoints: Define who writes each field
Publish initialized data with synchronization
Plan for stale data and participant failure
slides.narration: Suppose two participants share a record containing length and payload. Sharing makes the bytes reachable, but it does not guarantee that a reader sees a complete update. A writer could publish a new length before finishing the payload, and a reader could act on inconsistent fields. The communication design must specify ownership of updates and synchronization that establishes when the record is ready. An offset-based representation solves different virtual bases, not this publication problem. It also does not recover automatically if a writer stops halfway through an update. Separate address interpretation, data consistency, and recovery instead of asking the word shared to promise all three.

question.prompt: Does replacing stored pointers with offsets make simultaneous unsynchronized updates safe?
question.answer: No. Offsets solve address interpretation; synchronization and update protocols remain separate requirements.

slides.title: Debug an access at both language and system boundaries
keyPoints: Mapped and writable is weaker than a valid C++ access
Object lifetime and bounds still apply
Unmapping ends the mapping, not every stale reference
slides.narration: Imagine an array of four integers stored in a large writable page. Writing its fifth element can violate the language’s object bounds even though hardware permission checks allow the address. Now reverse the problem: a correctly typed pointer may refer to a region that was unmapped. The language-level type does not restore its mapping. Debugging needs both questions: does the object still exist with the required bounds, and does the environment permit this operation on its storage? Memory tools, checked boundaries, and clear ownership help answer different pieces. Do not treat the absence of a protection fault as proof that a C++ memory access was correct.

slides.title: Choose the smallest communication boundary
keyPoints: Messages can simplify ownership
Shared memory can reduce copying
Representation and lifetime determine the real cost
slides.narration: Shared memory is useful when repeated transfers would otherwise copy substantial data, but it introduces a shared-state protocol. A small occasional message may be easier to send through a pipe or socket, where ownership moves through a clearer boundary. Make the choice using required throughput, data size, update frequency, and failure handling. Our examples establish two facts: equal addresses do not imply equal storage, and unequal addresses do not prevent shared backing. Neither fact alone selects the best architecture. In a review, ask who initializes the region, who can remove it, how readers recognize a complete record, and how every offset is checked.
